newsitem.title: USA: IRS random audits to focus on 100 small issues.
newsitem.headline: IRS random audits to focus on 100 small issues.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service is launching its "random audit" program of tax-exempt bonds and asked field offices to focus in the next year on 100 small offerings between $1 and 10 million, an IRS official said.
"We have produced a work plan for our field offices for FY (fiscal year) '97, Marcus Owens, director of IRS' exempt organizations division, said in a telephone interview with Reuters.
"We have asked our field offices to expect to spend between seven and 10 percent of their examination resources on tax-exempt bond cases," Owens said.

Regarding the random audit portion of the work plan, Owens said the 100 cases are likely to involve conduit borrowers and to examine issues like their compliance with federal limits on capital expenses.
As for targeted audits, cases probably will fall into four categories, including offerings referred to IRS by informants, Owens said.
Another category is conduit bond issues, Owens said.
"Say there's a large hospital system under examination," he said. "I would expect that bonds issued by that hospital would be reviewed."
"But the reason for the audit being initiated may not have anything to do with bonds," Owens said.
Owens said field offices also will review some claims for arbitrage rebate refunds. He said he could not estimate how many claims would be reviewed.

"That will depend on what comes in the door," Owens said. "Obviously, all rebate claims will be processed" by IRS, he said. But while some will require a only a follow-up phone call to complete, others may involve a "more detailed review of books and records," Owens said.

Owens said: "We also will continue to see cases in the areas of potential non-compliance that we announced in January 1994 -- the open market purchases of Treasury obligations for advance refundings, that sort of thing.
IRS on July 19 said issuers of advance refunding bonds can enter into "closing agreements" with the Service to head off possibly having the interest on their bonds declared taxable.
Stunned market participants said the IRS "yield burning" notice could cost municipalities nationwide over $1 billion and trigger lawsuits against bond dealers, lawyers and financial advisers.
On random audits, Owens said the typical case might be a small business that is acting as a conduit borrower and dealing with issues like "limits on capital expenses."
Federal regulations currently limit the amount of capital expenses that a conduit borrower can make, including expenses financed by taxable bonds.
Owens said IRS probably will not focus on any other categories of bonds in 1997 under its random audit program.
"We expect 75 percent of audits will be completed by the end of 1997, with the whole project finished by March 1998," he said.
